takeaway: NCBlob applies low-subpacketization non-systematic MSR coding to locality-grouped small blobs and systematic Clay coding to large blobs, improving repairs with modest warm-read cost.
background: Warm blob stores keep immutable, occasionally read objects economically with erasure coding. Minimum-storage regenerating codes retain minimum redundancy while reducing the network traffic needed to rebuild a lost block.
villain: Systematic Clay codes divide blocks into exponentially many sub-blocks, producing scattered I/O and poor repair/degraded-read performance for small blobs. Non-systematic MSR codes use few sub-blocks but ordinarily decode multiple coded blocks for every normal read, amplifying I/O and computation.
approach: NCBlob co-encodes whole-blob or co-accessed-blob groups so one non-systematic decode serves data likely to be read together, and switches to Clay codes above a repair-cost threshold. Rotation-based helper selection and two-phase MDS checks sustain functional repair; sliced reads and grouped repair parallelize work.
impact: The hybrid architecture makes network-coding-style MSR practical for small warm objects while retaining direct systematic reads for large ones. It targets the dominant small-blob population without surrendering minimum storage or repair bandwidth.

evaluation.overview: Trace-derived cloud experiments measure sequential read throughput, merge-size sensitivity, single-block and full-node repair, degraded reads, encoding, network sensitivity, CPU use, and memory overhead across four coding parameters.
evaluation.implemented: An open-source 18.6-KSLoC C++ distributed prototype with client locality grouping, metadata/coordinator services, data agents, Redis control communication, Ceph/Jerasure coding, placement groups, slice-parallel reads, and group-parallel functional repair.
evaluation.setting: Twenty-two Alibaba Cloud nodes—one coordinator, 20 HDD agents, and one client—connected at 15 Gbps. A 60-GB sample of the 20.3-million-object Azure Blob Access Trace uses 95% small blobs by count and evaluates (6,4), (9,6), (12,8), and (14,10) codes over ten runs.

results.text: With locality grouping, NCBlob's reported read throughput is 2.1%–10.5% below Clay across examined cases; for (12,8) at 256-MB blocks it is 4.9× NCBlob without locality.
For 64-MB blocks, NCBlob cuts single-block repair time by up to 45.0% versus Clay; for (14,10) with 256-MB blocks it cuts full-node repair by 38.4% versus Clay and 76.4% versus Reed-Solomon.
For (14,10) and 256-MB blocks, the measured Clay degraded-read latency is 9.1× NCBlob's; NCBlob remains close to the Reed-Solomon/Clay hybrid across the tested degraded reads.

limitations: NCBlob depends on intra- or inter-blob access locality; without it the paper recommends systematic coding. Reads add decode work and lose 2.1%–10.5% throughput in tested cases, with higher CPU use. The design focuses on single failures and n−k≤4; perpetual existence is proved only for n−k=3, while n−k=4 relies on simulations. Evaluation uses a 60-GB trace sample, HDD cloud instances, and no production deployment.
phd_group_signal: This paper revisits a theoretically optimal but dismissed code by matching its drawbacks to workload locality and object-size distributions. It combines coding theory, I/O layout, distributed repair, trace analysis, and systems implementation.

claims.text: NCBlob either splits each independently read blob before cross-blob merging or first merges co-accessed blobs, ensuring that the extra objects reconstructed by a non-systematic read are useful or cacheable.

Each repair rotates the selected sub-block per helper, functionally generates a replacement, and accepts coefficients only after current and next-repair MDS checks; the paper proves existence for (k+3,k).
